title: Ποταμοῦ ἱκέτης
source: Homer, The Odyssey, Greek text of A. T. Murray (Loeb Classical Library; London: Heinemann, New York: Putnam, 1919), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg002.perseus-grc2, sha256 7d7ffafb6c51f8c2. Text as printed: Murray sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Two days and nights after his raft breaks apart, Odysseus at last sights the coast of Phaeacia, but finds a shore of bare rock with no harbour to receive him. A great wave dashes him against the cliffs and strips the skin from his hands; only Athena’s gift of presence of mind saves him from a death beyond what was allotted him. Swimming on, he finds the mouth of a river, prays to its unknown god, and is carried safely into calm water, where he collapses, revives, and returns Ino’s veil to the sea. Weighing the cold of the riverbank against the wild beasts of the wood, he crawls in under twin olive bushes and buries himself in leaves, and Athena pours sleep over his eyes to end his suffering.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα δύω νύκτας δύο τ’ ἤματα κύματι πηγῷ
πλάζετο, πολλὰ δέ οἱ κραδίη προτιόσσετ’ ὄλεθρον.
sentences.tr:
entha dyō nyktas dyo t’ ēmata kymati pēgōi
plazeto, polla de hoi kradiē protiosset’ olethron.
sentences.l:
There for two nights and two days, on the strong-packed wave,
he was driven, and much did his heart forebode destruction.
sentences.i: There, for two nights and two days, he was tossed on the heavy wave, and again and again his heart foreboded death.
sentences.n: ἔνθα is temporal, 'at that point', picking up after the storm has broken Odysseus's raft, told earlier in this book. δύω is the epic form of δύο 'two'. πηγός (dative κύματι πηγῷ) is a rare, disputed epithet: the ancient explanation ties it to πήγνυμι 'make fast, compact', giving 'massed, solid' water, though 'strong, mighty' has also been guessed; no certainty is possible. προτιόσσετ’ is προτιόσσετο, an unaugmented imperfect (Homer's past tenses regularly drop the augment ἐ-, a pattern you will meet constantly in this part) of the rare verb προτιόσσομαι 'look ahead to, forebode'. οἱ is the enclitic dative pronoun 'for him' (Attic αὐτῷ), extremely common in Homer.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ τρίτον ἦμαρ ἐυπλόκαμος τέλεσ’ Ἠώς,
καὶ τότ’ ἔπειτ’ ἄνεμος μὲν ἐπαύσατο ἠδὲ γαλήνη
ἔπλετο νηνεμίη·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē triton ēmar eyplokamos teles’ Ēōs,
kai tot’ epeit’ anemos men epausato ēde galēnē
epleto nēnemiē·
sentences.i: But when fine-plaited Dawn had brought the third day round, then at last the wind died down, and a windless calm settled;
sentences.n: ἐυπλόκαμος Ἠώς applies to Dawn the same epithet already fixed for Calypso's island nymph, 'fine-plaited'; the word does not change with its bearer, so it is kept the same for the goddess of the dawn. τέλεσ’ is τέλεσε, an unaugmented aorist of τελέω 'bring to an end, complete'. ἠδέ is the epic 'and'. ἔπλετο is an epic aorist of πέλομαι 'come to be, be', often no more than a colourless 'was'. νηνεμίη, 'windlessness', stands in apposition to γαλήνη 'calm': the two nouns together picture both the wind's dying and the sea's stillness.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρα σχεδὸν εἴσιδε γαῖαν
ὀξὺ μάλα προϊδών, μεγάλου ὑπὸ κύματος ἀρθείς.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ara schedon eiside gaian
oxy mala proïdōn, megalou hypo kymatos artheis.
sentences.l:
and he then, close by, caught sight of land,
looking very sharply ahead, lifted up by a great wave.
sentences.i: and he then caught sight of land close by, peering keenly ahead as he was lifted on a great wave.
sentences.n: ὁ δ’ ἄρα: ὁ is here a pronoun, 'he' (a pattern you will meet constantly — what looks like the Attic definite article is in Homer usually a demonstrative or personal pronoun). ἄρα is a common inferential particle, roughly 'then, as it turned out', one of a set of small particles (ῥα, ἄρ, νυ, περ, τε) that recur throughout and often resist exact translation. εἴσιδε is unaugmented (= εἰσεῖδε). προϊδών is the aorist participle of προοράω 'see before, see ahead'; ἀρθείς is the aorist passive participle of αἴρω 'lift', agreeing with ὁ.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἂν ἀσπάσιος βίοτος παίδεσσι φανήῃ
πατρός, ὃς ἐν νούσῳ κεῖται κρατέρ’ ἄλγεα πάσχων,
δηρὸν τηκόμενος, στυγερὸς δέ οἱ ἔχραε δαίμων,
ἀσπάσιον δ’ ἄρα τόν γε θεοὶ κακότητος ἔλυσαν,
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ an aspasios biotos paidessi phanēēi
patros, hos en nousōi keitai krater’ algea paschōn,
dēron tēkomenos, stygeros de hoi echrae daimōn,
aspasion d’ ara ton ge theoi kakotētos elysan,
sentences.l:
And as when, welcome, life to children should appear,
of a father, who in sickness lies, strong pains suffering,
long wasting away, and a hateful spirit has assailed him,
and welcome, then, that man the gods from his evil plight release,
sentences.i: Just as, when a father lies sick, worn down for a long time by strong pains and beset by some hateful power, the gods at last, to his children’s great relief, free him from his affliction and life becomes welcome to them again,
sentences.n: An extended simile, comparing the moment to ordinary human experience; it runs four lines to the correlative ὥς in the next unit ('as … so …'), cut here at the comma since a period would run past four lines. φανήῃ is an uncontracted epic subjunctive (Attic φανῇ), with ἄν giving a general 'whenever'. παίδεσσι is a dative plural in -εσσι(ν) (Attic -οις), one of the long epic dative endings (with -ῃσι(ν), -οισι(ν)) met often here. δαίμων is a vague 'power, spirit', not a named god, the usual word for what sends good or bad fortune. κακότητος is a genitive of separation with ἔλυσαν, 'released from evil'.

sentences.t:
ὣς Ὀδυσεῖ ἀσπαστὸν ἐείσατο γαῖα καὶ ὕλη,
νῆχε δ’ ἐπειγόμενος ποσὶν ἠπείρου ἐπιβῆναι.
sentences.tr:
hōs Odysei aspaston eeisato gaia kai hylē,
nēche d’ epeigomenos posin ēpeirou epibēnai.
sentences.l:
so to Odysseus welcome appeared the land and the woodland,
and he swam, pressing on, with his feet on the mainland to set foot.
sentences.i: just so, welcome to Odysseus now appeared the land and its woods, and he swam on, eager to set his feet on the mainland.
sentences.n: ὥς answers the ὡς of the previous unit, closing the simile. ἐείσατο is a reduplicated aorist of εἴδομαι 'appear, seem' (the augment doubled as ε-ε-, an epic form). Ὀδυσεῖ, with a single σ, is a dative of Ὀδυσεύς; Homer freely uses both Ὀδυσ- and Ὀδυσσ- as the metre requires, a variation you will meet again. ποσὶν … ἐπιβῆναι, 'to set foot with his feet', restates the action by its means, the feet; ἐπειγόμενος is a present participle, 'pressing on, hastening'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε τόσσον ἀπῆν ὅσσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας,
καὶ δὴ δοῦπον ἄκουσε ποτὶ σπιλάδεσσι θαλάσσης·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote tosson apēn hosson te gegōne boēsas,
kai dē doupon akouse poti spiladessi thalassēs·
sentences.l:
But when so far off he was as one shouting makes himself heard,
now indeed a booming he heard, against the reefs, of the sea;
sentences.i: But when he was still as far off as a man’s shout can carry, he now heard the sea booming against the reefs;
sentences.n: ὅσσον τε γέγωνε βοήσας is a fixed measure of distance, 'as far as a man calling out makes himself heard' (γέγωνε is a perfect with present sense, 'is audible, carries'); the epic τε marks it as a standing, general fact rather than a one-time detail, a use of 'epic τε' that recurs through the poem. σπιλάδεσσι is another dative plural in -εσσι(ν), 'against the reefs, crags'.

sentences.t:
ῥόχθει γὰρ μέγα κῦμα ποτὶ ξερὸν ἠπείροιο
δεινὸν ἐρευγόμενον, εἴλυτο δὲ πάνθ’ ἁλὸς ἄχνῃ·
sentences.tr:
rhochthei gar mega kyma poti xeron ēpeiroio
deinon ereugomenon, eilyto de panth’ halos achnēi·
sentences.l:
for a great wave was roaring against the dry land of the mainland,
belching terribly, and everything was wrapped in the foam of the sea;
sentences.i: for a great wave was roaring against the dry shore of the mainland, belching out terribly, and everything was wrapped in sea-foam;
sentences.n: ἠπείροιο is a genitive in -οιο (= -ου), the regular epic ending of the second declension you will meet constantly. ἐρευγόμενον, from ἐρεύγομαι 'belch, spew out', gives the wave an almost animal violence. εἴλυτο is a pluperfect passive of εἰλύω 'wrap, envelop', with intransitive, stative force, 'lay wrapped'. ἄχνη is properly chaff or froth; here it is sea-foam.

sentences.t: οὐ γὰρ ἔσαν λιμένες νηῶν ὄχοι, οὐδ’ ἐπιωγαί.
sentences.tr: ou gar esan limenes nēōn ochoi, oud’ epiōgai.
sentences.l: for there were no harbours, holders of ships, nor havens.
sentences.i: for there were no harbours to shelter ships, and no roadsteads.
sentences.n: ἔσαν is the epic form of ἦσαν 'were'. νηῶν ὄχοι, 'holders of ships', is a descriptive genitive phrase in apposition to λιμένες, picturing the harbour as something that 'holds' the ships safe. ἐπιωγή, 'a place of shelter from the wind', names a lesser refuge than λιμήν, a roadstead rather than a true harbour.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἀκταὶ προβλῆτες ἔσαν σπιλάδες τε πάγοι τε·
sentences.tr: all’ aktai problētes esan spilades te pagoi te·
sentences.l: But headlands jutting-forth there were, and reefs and crags;
sentences.i: There were only jutting headlands, reefs, and crags.
sentences.n: προβλής, 'jutting out, projecting', from προ- and βάλλω, describes a shoreline of bare rock with nowhere safe to land; the line completes, in three coordinated nouns, the picture begun by the harbourless coast of the line before.

sentences.t:
καὶ τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆος λύτο γούνατα καὶ φίλον ἦτορ,
ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
kai tot’ Odyssēos lyto gounata kai philon ētor,
ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l:
And then Odysseus’ knees were loosed, and his dear heart,
and, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And then Odysseus’ knees gave way, and his heart too, and, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: This whole two-line unit already stands, word for word, at 5.297–298 in odyssey-025, and is repeated here verbatim; its second line alone recurs twice more, once at 5.355 (odyssey-025, paired there with a different first line) and again here as a single line at 5.464 below. The wording is kept identical each time, as the house rule requires for a repeated line. γούνατα λύτο, 'the knees were loosed', is the regular Homeric formula for a sudden collapse of strength, whether from fear, weariness, or grief. ὀχθήσας is the aorist participle of ὀχθέω 'be vexed, be troubled'. μεγαλήτωρ, 'great-spirited', is kept apart from the different compound μεγάθυμος 'great-hearted'.

sentences.t:
ὤ μοι, ἐπεὶ δὴ γαῖαν ἀελπέα δῶκεν ἰδέσθαι
Ζεύς, καὶ δὴ τόδε λαῖτμα διατμήξας ἐπέρησα,
ἔκβασις οὔ πῃ φαίνεθ’ ἁλὸς πολιοῖο θύραζε·
sentences.tr:
ō moi, epei dē gaian aelpea dōken idesthai
Zeus, kai dē tode laitma diatmēxas eperēsa,
ekbasis ou pēi phaineth’ halos polioio thyraze·
sentences.i: “Ah me, now that Zeus has granted me to see land I had not hoped for, and I have cut across and crossed this gulf, nowhere does a way out of the grey sea onto dry land appear;
sentences.n: Murray prints no quotation marks around speeches, so t and l carry none; the mark shows this is the first of three such speeches here, and i alone adds quotation marks, opened here, closed at the speech's last unit. ὤ μοι is a cry of distress, kept apart from the fuller ὤ μοι ἐγὼ δειλός already fixed elsewhere. ἀελπής, 'unhoped for', is an alpha-privative compound of ἔλπομαι. διατμήξας is the aorist participle of διατμήγω 'cut through'; πολιοῖο repeats the fixed sea-epithet πολιὴ ἅλς 'the grey sea', genitive -οιο. θύραζε, 'to the outside', uses the directional suffix -δε (here -ζε after a vowel), met again here.
sentences.mark: Odysseus speaks to his own heart

sentences.t:
ἔκτοσθεν μὲν γὰρ πάγοι ὀξέες, ἀμφὶ δὲ κῦμα
βέβρυχεν ῥόθιον, λισσὴ δ’ ἀναδέδρομε πέτρη,
ἀγχιβαθὴς δὲ θάλασσα, καὶ οὔ πως ἔστι πόδεσσι
στήμεναι ἀμφοτέροισι καὶ ἐκφυγέειν κακότητα·
sentences.tr:
ektosthen men gar pagoi oxees, amphi de kyma
bebrychen rhothion, lissē d’ anadedrome petrē,
anchibathēs de thalassa, kai ou pōs esti podessi
stēmenai amphoteroisi kai ekphygeein kakotēta·
sentences.l:
for outside there are sharp crags, and around, the wave
roars, surging, and smooth rock has run up sheer,
and the sea is deep close to shore, and in no way is it possible with feet
to stand with both, and escape from evil plight;
sentences.i: for outside stand sharp crags, and all around the surge roars, and smooth rock rises sheer, and the sea is deep close in, so that there is no way to plant both feet and win free of this evil;
sentences.n: βέβρυχεν is a perfect with present force, of βρυχάομαι 'roar', properly of a lion, here of the surf. ἀναδέδρομε is a perfect of ἀνατρέχω 'run up', used of rock rising sheer from the water. ἀγχιβαθής, 'deep close by (the shore)', joins ἄγχι 'near' and βαθύς 'deep'. στήμεναι is an epic infinitive in -μεναι (Attic στῆναι); ἐκφυγέειν is the uncontracted epic infinitive (Attic ἐκφυγεῖν) — these longer epic infinitive endings, also found in -έμεν and -έμεναι, are common throughout Homer.

sentences.t:
μή πώς μ’ ἐκβαίνοντα βάλῃ λίθακι ποτὶ πέτρῃ
κῦμα μέγ’ ἁρπάξαν·
sentences.tr:
mē pōs m’ ekbainonta balēi lithaki poti petrēi
kyma meg’ harpaxan·
sentences.l:
lest somehow me, as I step out, it dash against a rock-mass, on a rock,
a great wave, having seized me;
sentences.i: for fear that, as I climb out, some great wave may seize me and dash me against the rocky mass;
sentences.n: μή πώς … βάλῃ is a clause of fearing, 'lest somehow it strike me' (with a verb of fearing left to be understood) — a construction that recurs through this speech. λίθακι is a rare word, found nowhere else in Homer, a noun meaning something like 'rocky mass, boulder'; its formation and exact sense are uncertain. As transmitted, the line is metrically irregular: λίθακι requires its final syllable, in the fifth foot, to be scanned long by a metrical lengthening otherwise unparalleled for this rare word, most likely because the poet needed a long syllable there and stretched an ordinarily short one to fit.

sentences.t: μελέη δέ μοι ἔσσεται ὁρμή.
sentences.tr: meleē de moi essetai hormē.
sentences.l: and vain will be, for me, my effort.
sentences.i: and my attempt will have been for nothing.
sentences.n: μελέη, 'vain, fruitless, wretched', modifies ὁρμή 'onrush, effort, attempt', the noun used elsewhere of a ship's or a runner's forward drive, here of Odysseus's attempt to land. ἔσσεται is the epic future of εἰμί (Attic ἔσται).

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κ’ ἔτι προτέρω παρανήξομαι, ἤν που ἐφεύρω
ἠιόνας τε παραπλῆγας λιμένας τε θαλάσσης,
sentences.tr:
ei de k’ eti proterō paranēxomai, ēn pou epheurō
ēionas te paraplēgas limenas te thalassēs,
sentences.l:
But if still further forward I swim along, in hope that somewhere I may find
beaches struck-by-the-surf, and harbours of the sea,
sentences.i: But if I swim on further still, in hopes of somewhere finding surf-beaten beaches and harbours of the sea,
sentences.n: κ(ε) with the future παρανήξομαι, and ἤν (= ἐάν) with the subjunctive ἐφεύρω, together build the conditional; κε/κεν does the work Attic gives to ἄν throughout Homer. παραπλήξ, 'struck on the side, beaten', describes shelving beaches where the surf breaks gently; the whole phrase ἠιόνας τε παραπλῆγας λιμένας τε θαλάσσης recurs unchanged at line 440 of this same part, and its English is kept identical both times.

sentences.t:
δείδω μή μ’ ἐξαῦτις ἀναρπάξασα θύελλα
πόντον ἐπ’ ἰχθυόεντα φέρῃ βαρέα στενάχοντα,
ἠέ τί μοι καὶ κῆτος ἐπισσεύῃ μέγα δαίμων
ἐξ ἁλός, οἷά τε πολλὰ τρέφει κλυτὸς Ἀμφιτρίτη·
sentences.tr:
deidō mē m’ exautis anarpaxasa thyella
ponton ep’ ichthyoenta pherēi barea stenachonta,
ēe ti moi kai kētos episseuēi mega daimōn
ex halos, hoia te polla trephei klytos Amphitritē·
sentences.l:
I fear lest me once again, having snatched me up, a storm-blast
over the fish-teeming sea should carry, groaning heavily,
or lest on me too some great sea-monster a power should send
out of the sea, such as many famous Amphitrite feeds;
sentences.i: I am afraid that a storm-blast may snatch me up again and carry me, groaning heavily, out over the fish-teeming sea, or that some power may send some great sea-monster against me out of the sea, of the kind that famous Amphitrite breeds in plenty;
sentences.n: δείδω governs two parallel clauses of fearing, μή … φέρῃ and ἠέ … ἐπισσεύῃ. θύελλα 'storm-blast' is kept distinct from the related noun ἄελλα 'blast', already fixed elsewhere in the poem. κῆτος is any large sea-creature, a 'sea-monster', not necessarily a whale. κλυτὸς Ἀμφιτρίτη keeps κλυτός as 'famous', its fixed rendering throughout (compare κλυτὰ δώματα and κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος below), with Amphitrite named as Poseidon's consort, standing here, by a common extension, for the sea and its creatures generally.

sentences.t: οἶδα γάρ, ὥς μοι ὀδώδυσται κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος.
sentences.tr: oida gar, hōs moi odōdystai klytos ennosigaios.
sentences.l: for I know how against me is enraged the famous earth-shaker.”
sentences.i: for I know how the famous earth-shaker rages against me.”
sentences.n: This closes the first of Odysseus's three speeches to his own heart in this part; i closes the quotation mark opened at the speech's first unit. ὀδώδυσται is a perfect of ὀδύσσομαι 'be angry at, hate', the same rare verb that puns on the hero's own name at 1.62 (τί νύ οἱ τόσον ὠδύσαο). κλυτὸς ἐννοσίγαιος, 'the famous earth-shaker', is a variant on the already-fixed κρείων ἐνοσίχθων 'the lord earth-shaker': a different compound of the same root (built on γαῖα rather than χθών) with a different fixed epithet, κλυτός 'famous' in place of κρείων 'lord', kept as its own distinct formula.

sentences.t:
ἧος ὁ ταῦθ’ ὥρμαινε κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν,
τόφρα δέ μιν μέγα κῦμα φέρε τρηχεῖαν ἐπ’ ἀκτήν.
sentences.tr:
hēos ho tauth’ hōrmaine kata phrena kai kata thymon,
tophra de min mega kyma phere trēcheian ep’ aktēn.
sentences.l:
While he was pondering these things in mind and in heart,
meanwhile a great wave was carrying him onto the rugged shore.
sentences.i: While he was turning this over in his mind and heart, a great wave was carrying him toward the rugged shore.
sentences.n: Line 424 is itself an exact repeat of a line already published (odyssey-015), where the same formula introduces Helen's entrance; that line's own English, 'While he was pondering these things in mind and in heart,', is reused here unchanged, though its continuation there is unrelated to this passage. ἧος … τόφρα is the regular Homeric correlative 'while … meanwhile', marking simultaneous action. κατὰ φρένα καὶ κατὰ θυμόν is the fixed formula 'in mind and in heart'.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κ’ ἀπὸ ῥινοὺς δρύφθη, σὺν δ’ ὀστέ’ ἀράχθη,
εἰ μὴ ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε θεά, γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr:
entha k’ apo rhinous dryphthē, syn d’ oste’ arachthē,
ei mē epi phresi thēke thea, glaukōpis Athēnē·
sentences.l:
There would his skin have been stripped off, and together his bones been shattered,
had not upon his mind put it the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena;
sentences.i: There his skin would have been torn away and his bones crushed together, had not the goddess, gleaming-eyed Athena, put a thought into his mind;
sentences.n: κ(ε) with the aorist indicatives δρύφθη and ἀράχθη marks an unreal past condition ('would have been…'), answered by the εἰ μή clause. σύν … ἀράχθη is tmesis, the preverb σύν standing apart from its verb (συναράσσω 'dash together, shatter'), a pattern you will meet again in this part. ἐπὶ φρεσὶ θῆκε, 'put into his wits', is the usual way of saying a god prompts a sudden right idea; γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη keeps the fixed rendering 'gleaming-eyed Athena'.

sentences.t:
ἀμφοτέρῃσι δὲ χερσὶν ἐπεσσύμενος λάβε πέτρης,
τῆς ἔχετο στενάχων, ἧος μέγα κῦμα παρῆλθε.
sentences.tr:
amphoterēisi de chersin epessymenos labe petrēs,
tēs echeto stenachōn, hēos mega kyma parēlthe.
sentences.l:
and with both hands, rushing forward, he seized a rock,
to which he clung, groaning, until the great wave had passed by.
sentences.i: with both hands he rushed forward and seized hold of a rock, and clung to it groaning until the great wave had gone past.
sentences.n: ἀμφοτέρῃσι is a dative plural in -ῃσι(ν) (Attic -αις). ἐπεσσύμενος is a perfect participle of ἐπισεύω, 'rushing on, in a rush'; λάβε and ἔχετο both take the genitive πέτρης, 'took hold of, held onto'. ἧος (= ἕως) 'until' is the same conjunction met just above as 'while'.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν ὣς ὑπάλυξε, παλιρρόθιον δέ μιν αὖτις
πλῆξεν ἐπεσσύμενον, τηλοῦ δέ μιν ἔμβαλε πόντῳ.
sentences.tr:
kai to men hōs hypalyxe, palirrothion de min autis
plēxen epessymenon, tēlou de min embale pontōi.
sentences.l:
And that, indeed, thus he escaped, but the backwash-wave, him, again,
struck, rushing on, and far off it threw him into the open sea.
sentences.i: So he escaped that wave, but the backwash struck him again as it rushed back, and flung him far out into the sea.
sentences.n: ὑπάλυξε is the aorist of ὑπαλύσκω 'escape, avoid', with τὸ μέν, 'that', referring back to the wave just described. παλιρρόθιον, 'flowing back, backwash', joins πάλιν 'back' and ῥόθος 'rushing sound, surge'. τηλοῦ … πόντῳ, 'far off, into the sea', repeats exactly the danger of open water Odysseus had feared in his own speech just before.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε πουλύποδος θαλάμης ἐξελκομένοιο
πρὸς κοτυληδονόφιν πυκιναὶ λάιγγες ἔχονται,
ὣς τοῦ πρὸς πέτρῃσι θρασειάων ἀπὸ χειρῶν
ῥινοὶ ἀπέδρυφθεν·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote poulypodos thalamēs exelkomenoio
pros kotylēdonophin pykinai lainges echontai,
hōs tou pros petrēisi thraseiaōn apo cheirōn
rhinoi apedryphthen·
sentences.l:
And as when, of an octopus dragged from its lair,
to its suckers close-packed pebbles cling,
so from his hands, bold as they were, against the rocks,
the skin was stripped away;
sentences.i: And as, when an octopus is dragged from its lair, thick-clustered pebbles cling to its suckers, so now the skin was torn from his bold hands against the rocks;
sentences.n: A second simile matches Odysseus's ordeal to the everyday sight of an octopus torn from its den with pebbles still stuck to its suckers, a vivid, homely image kept fixed as a set: octopus, lair, suckers, and clinging pebbles are all likely to recur in comparable Homeric similes. πουλύπους is the epic form of πολύπους 'octopus' (with epic lengthening που- for πο-). κοτυληδονόφιν is an old case-form in -φι(ν) doing service as a dative, 'to its suckers' (from κοτυληδών, properly a cup-shaped hollow); the suffix -φι recurs in Homer for several cases. λάιγγες, 'pebbles', is a rare noun found almost only in this simile.

sentences.t: τὸν δὲ μέγα κῦμα κάλυψεν.
sentences.tr: ton de mega kyma kalypsen.
sentences.l: and the great wave covered him.
sentences.i: and the great wave closed over him.
sentences.n: κάλυψεν, aorist of καλύπτω 'cover, hide', closes the octopus-simile with a plain statement of the danger: Odysseus, now bleeding from stripped hands, is submerged by the wave. The same verb returns, of a gentler covering, when he buries himself under leaves at the end of this part (5.491).

sentences.t:
ἔνθα κε δὴ δύστηνος ὑπὲρ μόρον ὤλετ’ Ὀδυσσεύς,
εἰ μὴ ἐπιφροσύνην δῶκε γλαυκῶπις Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr:
entha ke dē dystēnos hyper moron ōlet’ Odysseus,
ei mē epiphrosynēn dōke glaukōpis Athēnē.
sentences.l:
There then wretched, beyond portion, would Odysseus have perished,
had not presence of mind given gleaming-eyed Athena.
sentences.i: There wretched Odysseus would have died beyond what was allotted him, had not gleaming-eyed Athena given him presence of mind.
sentences.n: δύστηνος keeps the house rendering 'wretched', and ὑπὲρ μόρον the fixed 'beyond portion' / 'beyond what was allotted' — the same phrase ὑπὲρ μόρον already fixed in the pilot part for Aegisthus's offense (1.35, 'beyond what was allotted'), now applied, strikingly, to the poem's own hero (δύστηνος itself is not paired with it there): a near-death the plan of the gods does not in fact allow. κε with the aorist ὤλετ(ο) marks another unreal past condition, as at line 426 above. ἐπιφροσύνη, 'presence of mind, a timely thought', is a rare abstract noun (from ἐπίφρων) naming the sudden practical wit that lets a person act rightly in a crisis, distinct from the settled good judgement of πεπνυμένος 'prudent', already fixed elsewhere for a different word; see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
κύματος ἐξαναδύς, τά τ’ ἐρεύγεται ἤπειρόνδε,
νῆχε παρέξ, ἐς γαῖαν ὁρώμενος, εἴ που ἐφεύροι
ἠιόνας τε παραπλῆγας λιμένας τε θαλάσσης.
sentences.tr:
kymatos exanadys, ta t’ ereugetai ēpeironde,
nēche parex, es gaian horōmenos, ei pou epheuroi
ēionas te paraplēgas limenas te thalassēs.
sentences.l:
Rising up out of the wave, which belches itself onto the mainland,
he swam alongside, looking toward the land, in hope that he might somewhere find
surf-beaten beaches and harbours of the sea.
sentences.i: Rising up out of the surf that spews itself onto the shore, he swam along outside it, watching the land in hope of somewhere finding surf-beaten beaches and harbours of the sea.
sentences.n: ἐξαναδύς is the aorist participle of ἐξαναδύομαι 'rise up out of'. ἤπειρόνδε again shows the directional suffix -δε, 'onto the mainland'. The last line repeats verbatim the formula already used at line 418 of this same speech; its English is kept identical, since a repeated line takes the same rendering wherever it recurs, even within a single part.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ποταμοῖο κατὰ στόμα καλλιρόοιο
ἷξε νέων, τῇ δή οἱ ἐείσατο χῶρος ἄριστος,
λεῖος πετράων, καὶ ἐπὶ σκέπας ἦν ἀνέμοιο,
ἔγνω δὲ προρέοντα καὶ εὔξατο ὃν κατὰ θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē potamoio kata stoma kallirooio
hixe neōn, tēi dē hoi eeisato chōros aristos,
leios petraōn, kai epi skepas ēn anemoio,
egnō de proreonta kai euxato hon kata thymon·
sentences.l:
But when indeed at the mouth of a river fair-flowing
he arrived, swimming, where indeed to him it seemed the best place,
smooth of rocks, and where there was shelter from the wind,
he recognized it flowing forth, and prayed in his own heart:
sentences.i: But when, still swimming, he reached the mouth of a fair-flowing river, at the place that seemed to him best, free of rocks and sheltered from the wind, he recognized it as a river’s outflow and prayed in his own heart:
sentences.n: καλλιρόοιο is another genitive in -οιο, 'of fair flow'. προρέοντα, 'flowing forward', names the fresh water Odysseus recognizes at the river's mouth, visibly distinct from the salt sea around it — and it is exactly this recognition that leads him to address it as a god in the next unit. ὃν κατὰ θυμόν, 'in his own heart', is the possessive ὅς again, easily mistaken for the relative pronoun.

sentences.t: κλῦθι, ἄναξ, ὅτις ἐσσί·
sentences.tr: klythi, anax, hotis essi·
sentences.l: “Hear me, lord, whoever you are;
sentences.i: “Hear me, lord, whoever you may be;
sentences.n: This opens Odysseus's second speech in the part, now addressed outward to the river itself as a god — a prayer, not a speech to his own heart — and the mark and the opening quotation mark are both set here. κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω 'hear'. ἄναξ, ὅτις ἐσσί, 'lord, whoever you are', is a striking formula for addressing an unnamed local god by his function alone, a common feature of river- and place-cult; it is fixed now as a likely recurring prayer-opening, see new-renderings.md. ἐσσί is the epic second singular of εἰμί (Attic εἶ).

sentences.t:
πολύλλιστον δέ σ’ ἱκάνω,
φεύγων ἐκ πόντοιο Ποσειδάωνος ἐνιπάς.
sentences.tr:
polylliston de s’ hikanō,
pheugōn ek pontoio Poseidaōnos enipas.
sentences.l:
and much-entreated I come to you,
fleeing, out of the sea, from the threats of Poseidon.
sentences.i: much-prayed-to as you are, I come to you, fleeing from the sea and from the threats of Poseidon.
sentences.n: πολύλλιστος, 'much prayed to, much besought', built on λίσσομαι 'entreat', pictures the river as one who regularly receives such prayers from travellers; it agrees with σε 'you'. ἐνιπή is properly a 'rebuke, scolding', but is used here, by extension, of Poseidon's violent chastisement at sea, the punishing action itself rather than mere words.

sentences.t:
αἰδοῖος μέν τ’ ἐστὶ καὶ ἀθανάτοισι θεοῖσιν
ἀνδρῶν ὅς τις ἵκηται ἀλώμενος, ὡς καὶ ἐγὼ νῦν
σόν τε ῥόον σά τε γούναθ’ ἱκάνω πολλὰ μογήσας.
sentences.tr:
aidoios men t’ esti kai athanatoisi theoisin
andrōn hos tis hikētai alōmenos, hōs kai egō nyn
son te rhoon sa te gounath’ hikanō polla mogēsas.
sentences.l:
Revered indeed even to the immortal gods
is that man, whoever, wandering, comes as a suppliant, as now I too
your stream and your knees approach, having toiled much.
sentences.i: Even the immortal gods hold in respect whatever man comes to them as a wanderer in need, as I now come to your stream and clasp your knees, after much toil.
sentences.n: This states the custom underlying the whole scene: a suppliant (ἱκέτης) in need stands under a god-given protection, and to wrong him is an offence reaching up to Zeus and the gods generally, the same principle that governs a guest's reception elsewhere in this poem. ἀθανάτοισι is a dative plural in -οισι(ν). ἵκηται is a subjunctive in a general relative clause, 'whoever comes'. γούναθ’ ἱκάνω, 'I come to your knees', uses the standard gesture-language of supplication, clasping the knees of the one addressed, carried over here to a river that has no literal knees to clasp.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἐλέαιρε, ἄναξ·
sentences.tr: all’ eleaire, anax·
sentences.l: But have pity, lord;
sentences.i: But have pity on me, lord;
sentences.n: ἐλέαιρε is the imperative of ἐλεαίρω, the epic by-form of ἐλεέω 'pity', already met in the pilot part of the gods' pity for Odysseus (1.19); the same verb here becomes a direct plea.

sentences.t: ἱκέτης δέ τοι εὔχομαι εἶναι.
sentences.tr: hiketēs de toi euchomai einai.
sentences.l: your suppliant I declare myself to be.”
sentences.i: I declare myself your suppliant.”
sentences.n: This closes Odysseus's prayer; i closes the quotation mark opened at 'Hear me, lord'. εὔχομαι here is not 'pray' but its other common Homeric sense, 'declare, avow, claim to be', a formal self-identification that places him under the protection due to a suppliant's status; the whole line is fixed as a likely recurring formula, see new-renderings.md.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάθ’, ὁ δ’ αὐτίκα παῦσεν ἑὸν ῥόον, ἔσχε δὲ κῦμα,
πρόσθε δέ οἱ ποίησε γαλήνην, τὸν δ’ ἐσάωσεν
ἐς ποταμοῦ προχοάς.
sentences.tr:
hōs phath’, ho d’ autika pausen heon rhoon, esche de kyma,
prosthe de hoi poiēse galēnēn, ton d’ esaōsen
es potamou prochoas.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and he at once stopped his own stream, and checked the wave,
and before him made a calm, and him he brought safely
into the river’s outflow.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the river at once checked its own current, held back its wave, made a calm before him, and brought him safely into the river’s mouth.
sentences.n: ὣς φάθ(ε), 'so he spoke', is the regular closing formula for a speech, already fixed in the pilot part as ὣς φάτο; here, unusually, the god addressed answers the prayer with action rather than with words of his own. ἑόν is the possessive 'his own' (= ἑαυτοῦ). προχοαί, 'outflowings, the place where a river pours out', is a plural noun used for a single feature, as with σπέσσι 'caves' in the pilot part.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ ἄμφω γούνατ’ ἔκαμψε
χεῖράς τε στιβαράς.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ amphō gounat’ ekampse
cheiras te stibaras.
sentences.l:
And he then both his knees bent,
and his sturdy hands.
sentences.i: And he sank down, bending both his knees and his strong hands beneath him.
sentences.n: ἔκαμψε, 'bent', governs both γούνατα 'knees' and χεῖρας 'hands' together, picturing Odysseus collapsing forward onto hands and knees at once, utterly spent — the same collapse the formula 'his knees were loosed' pictured more briefly at line 406.

sentences.t: ἁλὶ γὰρ δέδμητο φίλον κῆρ.
sentences.tr: hali gar dedmēto philon kēr.
sentences.l: for by the sea was overpowered his dear heart.
sentences.i: for his heart was overwhelmed by the sea.
sentences.n: δέδμητο is a pluperfect passive of δάμνημι 'subdue, overpower', with ἁλί, 'by the sea', as the agent — the same power over him that his own fears in the first speech had already voiced.

sentences.t:
ᾤδεε δὲ χρόα πάντα, θάλασσα δὲ κήκιε πολλὴ
ἂν στόμα τε ῥῖνάς θ’·
sentences.tr:
ōidee de chroa panta, thalassa de kēkie pollē
an stoma te rhinas th’·
sentences.l:
And swollen was all his flesh, and the sea kept oozing out, much of it,
up through his mouth and his nostrils;
sentences.i: His whole body was swollen, and quantities of sea-water kept oozing up through his mouth and nostrils;
sentences.n: ᾤδεε is a pluperfect of οἰδέω 'swell', with present force, 'was swollen'; χρόα πάντα, 'all his flesh', is an accusative of respect. κήκιε is an imperfect of κηκίω 'ooze, trickle out', a vivid, near-clinical detail of near-drowning kept fixed for the phrase 'his flesh swelled all over', see new-renderings.md; ἀνά (ἄν before a vowel) with στόμα and ῥῖνας pictures the water forced back up and out through mouth and nose.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἄρ’ ἄπνευστος καὶ ἄναυδος
κεῖτ’ ὀλιγηπελέων, κάματος δέ μιν αἰνὸς ἵκανεν.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ apneustos kai anaudos
keit’ oligēpeleōn, kamatos de min ainos hikanen.
sentences.l:
and he then, breathless and speechless,
lay, faint with little strength, and dread weariness came upon him.
sentences.i: and he lay there, not breathing, not able to speak, faint and barely conscious, as a terrible weariness overcame him.
sentences.n: ὀλιγηπελέων, 'faint, having little strength' (from ὀλίγος 'little' and a rare stem for strength), describes a state on the edge of collapse; the related noun ὀλιγηπελίη, 'faintness', recurs at line 468 below, and both are kept to one consistent rendering, 'faint' / 'faintness', throughout — see new-renderings.md. ἄπνευστος and ἄναυδος are both alpha-privative adjectives, 'without breath' and 'without voice'.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δή ῥ’ ἄμπνυτο καὶ ἐς φρένα θυμὸς ἀγέρθη,
καὶ τότε δὴ κρήδεμνον ἀπὸ ἕο λῦσε θεοῖο.
sentences.tr:
all’ hote dē rh’ ampnyto kai es phrena thymos agerthē,
kai tote dē krēdemnon apo heo lyse theoio.
sentences.l:
But when indeed he revived, and into his wits his spirit was gathered back,
then indeed the head-veil from himself he loosed, the goddess’s.
sentences.i: But when he had revived, and his spirit had gathered itself back into his wits, then at last he untied from himself the goddess’s head-veil.
sentences.n: ἄμπνυτο is an unaugmented past tense of ἀναπνέω/ἄμπνυμαι 'recover breath, revive'. κρήδεμνον, 'head-veil', keeps the rendering already fixed for the veil the sea-goddess Ino gave Odysseus earlier in this book, now to be returned since he is safe. θεοῖο is the genitive of θεά 'goddess', referring to Ino, not to the river.

sentences.t:
καὶ τὸ μὲν ἐς ποταμὸν ἁλιμυρήεντα μεθῆκεν,
ἂψ δ’ ἔφερεν μέγα κῦμα κατὰ ῥόον, αἶψα δ’ ἄρ’ Ἰνὼ
δέξατο χερσὶ φίλῃσιν·
sentences.tr:
kai to men es potamon halimyrēenta methēken,
aps d’ epheren mega kyma kata rhoon, aipsa d’ ar’ Inō
dexato chersi philēisin·
sentences.i: He let it go into the river that runs down to the sea, and a great wave carried it back down the current, and at once Ino caught it with her own hands;
sentences.n: ἁλιμυρήεις, 'flowing to the salt sea', describes the river at the point where fresh water meets salt. μεθῆκεν is the aorist of μεθίημι 'let go, release'. Ino is named here alone, without a fuller epithet, since she has already been introduced by name and title earlier in this book; her gift, the head-veil, now returns to her on the current, exactly as she instructed when she gave it.

sentences.t:
ὁ δ’ ἐκ ποταμοῖο λιασθεὶς
σχοίνῳ ὑπεκλίνθη, κύσε δὲ ζείδωρον ἄρουραν.
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ek potamoio liastheis
schoinōi hypeklinthē, kyse de zeidōron arouran.
sentences.l:
and he, from the river having drawn back,
sank down beneath the rushes, and kissed the grain-giving plough-land.
sentences.i: and he drew back from the river, sank down among the rushes, and kissed the grain-giving plough-land.
sentences.n: λιασθείς is the aorist passive participle of λιάζομαι 'turn aside, draw back'. ζείδωρον ἄρουραν keeps unchanged the rendering already fixed for this formula, 'the grain-giving plough-land'. The gesture of kissing the earth marks the sheer relief of reaching solid land at last, after two days and nights in the sea.

sentences.t: ὀχθήσας δ’ ἄρα εἶπε πρὸς ὃν μεγαλήτορα θυμόν·
sentences.tr: ochthēsas d’ ara eipe pros hon megalētora thymon·
sentences.l: And, vexed, he then spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.i: And, troubled, he spoke to his own great-spirited heart:
sentences.n: This single line repeats, word for word, the second half of the two-line formula already used at line 406 of this part (and published earlier at 5.298 = 5.355); the wording is kept identical, as required for a repeated line, even though the paired first line does not accompany it this time, and only the initial capital changes since the line now opens its own sentence.

sentences.t: ὤ μοι ἐγώ, τί πάθω;
sentences.tr: ō moi egō, ti pathō;
sentences.l: “Ah me, what am I to suffer?
sentences.i: “Ah me, what is to become of me?
sentences.n: This opens the third and last of Odysseus's speeches to his own heart in this part. τί πάθω is a deliberative subjunctive, 'what am I to suffer, to experience', the regular Homeric way of asking what course to take in distress.
sentences.mark: Odysseus speaks to his own heart

sentences.t: τί νύ μοι μήκιστα γένηται;
sentences.tr: ti ny moi mēkista genētai;
sentences.l: What now, in the end, is to become of me?
sentences.i: What in the end is to happen to me?
sentences.n: μήκιστα is a superlative adverb, 'at the very longest, in the end', from μῆκος 'length'; the two rhetorical questions together are a conventional opening of distress before a person weighs alternatives, as Odysseus now does in the lines that follow.

sentences.t:
εἰ μέν κ’ ἐν ποταμῷ δυσκηδέα νύκτα φυλάσσω,
μή μ’ ἄμυδις στίβη τε κακὴ καὶ θῆλυς ἐέρση
ἐξ ὀλιγηπελίης δαμάσῃ κεκαφηότα θυμόν·
sentences.tr:
ei men k’ en potamōi dyskēdea nykta phylassō,
mē m’ amydis stibē te kakē kai thēlys eersē
ex oligēpeliēs damasēi kekaphēota thymon·
sentences.i: If I spend a troubled night here by the river, I am afraid that harsh frost and soft dew together may finish off my exhausted, gasping spirit in my weakened state;
sentences.n: δυσκηδής, 'bringing hard distress', is a rare compound (δυσ- + κῆδος 'care, grief'). ἐξ ὀλιγηπελίης repeats, as a noun, the 'faintness' met as a participle at line 457 above. κεκαφηότα is a rare perfect participle whose exact derivation is disputed — perhaps from an old verb meaning 'breathe out, gasp', giving 'spent of breath, gasping'; the sense 'exhausted, gasping' is followed here, but the formation itself is not fully understood.

sentences.t: αὔρη δ’ ἐκ ποταμοῦ ψυχρὴ πνέει ἠῶθι πρό.
sentences.tr: aurē d’ ek potamou psychrē pneei ēōthi pro.
sentences.l: and a breeze from the river, cold, blows before the dawn.
sentences.i: and a cold breeze blows off the river before daybreak.
sentences.n: ἠῶθι πρό, 'before dawn, at the point before daybreak': ἠῶθι is itself ἠώς 'dawn' with the place-suffix -θι (already seen in θύραζε-type words) added, giving 'at dawn'; πρό then adds 'before, in advance of'.

sentences.t:
εἰ δέ κεν ἐς κλιτὺν ἀναβὰς καὶ δάσκιον ὕλην
θάμνοις ἐν πυκινοῖσι καταδράθω, εἴ με μεθείη
ῥῖγος καὶ κάματος, γλυκερὸς δέ μοι ὕπνος ἐπέλθῃ,
δείδω, μὴ θήρεσσιν ἕλωρ καὶ κύρμα γένωμαι.
sentences.tr:
ei de ken es klityn anabas kai daskion hylēn
thamnois en pykinoisi katadrathō, ei me metheiē
rhigos kai kamatos, glykeros de moi hypnos epelthēi,
deidō, mē thēressin helōr kai kyrma genōmai.
sentences.l:
But if, on the other hand, up a slope having climbed, and into shadowy woodland,
in thick bushes I lie down to sleep, in hope that it might let me go,
the chill and the weariness, and sweet sleep might come over me,
I fear lest to wild beasts a prey and a spoil I become.”
sentences.i: But if instead I climb up the slope into the shadowy woods and lie down to sleep among thick bushes, in hope that the cold and my weariness may let me go and sweet sleep come over me, I am afraid I may become the prey and spoil of wild animals.”
sentences.n: This closes Odysseus's third speech; i closes the quote opened at 'Ah me, what is to become of me?'. καταδράθω is an aorist subjunctive of καταδαρθάνω 'lie down to sleep'; εἴ με μεθείη is an optative wish, 'in hope that it might release me'. The line shows a real ambiguity, but not where it first appears: ἐς already ends in σ and is long regardless of what follows, so κλιτύν's κλ gives no real choice; the two scansions come instead from δάσκιον, whose -ιο- may be two syllables or drawn together by synizesis, an ordinary licence — either way the line scans, and this is no fault in the text.

sentences.t: ὣς ἄρα οἱ φρονέοντι δοάσσατο κέρδιον εἶναι·
sentences.tr: hōs ara hoi phroneonti doassato kerdion einai·
sentences.l: So then, to him as he considered, it seemed better to be;
sentences.i: So, as he weighed it, this seemed to him the better course;
sentences.n: δοάσσατο is a rare aorist (related to δοκέω) meaning 'it seemed'; φρονέοντι is a dative participle agreeing with οἱ, 'to him thinking it over'. κέρδιον, a comparative of κέρδος 'gain, advantage', is 'more profitable, better' — the poem does not restate here which of the two options in the preceding speech Odysseus chooses, since only one is then described.

sentences.t: βῆ ῥ’ ἴμεν εἰς ὕλην·
sentences.tr: bē rh’ imen eis hylēn·
sentences.l: He set out to go into the woodland;
sentences.i: He set out for the woods;
sentences.n: βῆ … ἴμεν, 'he went to go', pairs a finite aorist of βαίνω with a complementary infinitive of εἶμι, the regular Homeric idiom for setting out on foot, kept to the house rendering 'set out to go' / 'set out for'. εἰς is the fuller epic by-form of ἐς, both found freely side by side in Homer.

sentences.t:
τὴν δὲ σχεδὸν ὕδατος εὗρεν
ἐν περιφαινομένῳ·
sentences.tr:
tēn de schedon hydatos heuren
en periphainomenōi·
sentences.l:
and it, close to the water, he found,
in a place open on every side;
sentences.i: and he found it close to the water, in a spot open all around;
sentences.n: τὴν … εὗρεν, 'he found it', refers ahead to ὕλην 'the woodland' just named. ἐν περιφαινομένῳ, 'in a place showing round about, open to view on every side', is a present passive participle used as a substantive, describing a clearing visible from all directions.

sentences.t:
δοιοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ ὑπήλυθε θάμνους,
ἐξ ὁμόθεν πεφυῶτας·
sentences.tr:
doious d’ ar’ hypēlythe thamnous,
ex homothen pephyōtas·
sentences.l:
and two bushes then he went in under,
grown from the same root;
sentences.i: and he crept in beneath two bushes that grew up from the same root;
sentences.n: ὑπήλυθε is an unaugmented aorist of ὑπέρχομαι 'go in under, creep beneath'. πεφυῶτας is a perfect participle of φύω 'grow', 'having grown', agreeing with θάμνους; ἐξ ὁμόθεν, 'from the same place', describes the two bushes as springing from one root, the twin bushes of this passage's famous image.

sentences.t: ὁ μὲν φυλίης, ὁ δ’ ἐλαίης.
sentences.tr: ho men phyliēs, ho d’ elaiēs.
sentences.l: the one a wild-olive, and the other an olive.
sentences.i: one a wild olive, the other a cultivated olive.
sentences.n: φυλίη is the wild olive, ἐλαίη the cultivated olive tree; the pairing of the wild and the tended tree, grown together from one root, has struck readers since antiquity as an emblem of Odysseus himself, poised between the wild world of his wanderings and the ordered household he is still trying to reach.

sentences.t:
τοὺς μὲν ἄρ’ οὔτ’ ἀνέμων διάη μένος ὑγρὸν ἀέντων,
οὔτε ποτ’ ἠέλιος φαέθων ἀκτῖσιν ἔβαλλεν,
οὔτ’ ὄμβρος περάασκε διαμπερές·
sentences.tr:
tous men ar’ out’ anemōn diaē menos hygron aentōn,
oute pot’ ēelios phaethōn aktisin eballen,
out’ ombros peraaske diamperes·
sentences.i: Through these bushes no wind’s moist force ever blew, no shining sun ever struck with its rays, and no rain ever soaked all the way through;
sentences.n: διάη is a rare aorist subjunctive of διάημι 'blow through', with the redundant genitive ἀνέμων … ἀέντων, 'of winds blowing', a construction that piles up the idea of wind for emphasis. περάασκε is an iterative imperfect in -ασκε, a form marking repeated or habitual past action ('used to pass through'), freely formed by Homer from many verbs; here it describes the bushes' standing property of never letting rain soak through, not one occasion.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα πυκνοὶ
ἀλλήλοισιν ἔφυν ἐπαμοιβαδίς·
sentences.tr:
hōs ara pyknoi
allēloisin ephyn epamoibadis·
sentences.l:
so, then, thick
into one another they had grown, alternately;
sentences.i: so thickly had they grown together, branch within branch;
sentences.n: ἔφυν is the intransitive aorist of φύω, 'grew, had grown'. ἐπαμοιβαδίς, 'alternately, in turn', is an adverb found almost only here, describing how the two trees' branches interweave.

sentences.t:
οὓς ὑπ’ Ὀδυσσεὺς
δύσετ’.
sentences.tr:
hous hyp’ Odysseus
dyset’.
sentences.l:
beneath which Odysseus
sank down.
sentences.i: and beneath them Odysseus made his way in.
sentences.n: δύσετ(ο) is an unaugmented aorist middle of δύω 'sink into, enter'; ὑπό, here in tmesis with the verb, is 'underneath, in among'.

sentences.t:
ἄφαρ δ’ εὐνὴν ἐπαμήσατο χερσὶ φίλῃσιν
εὐρεῖαν·
sentences.tr:
aphar d’ eunēn epamēsato chersi philēisin
eureian·
sentences.l:
and at once a bed he heaped up with his own dear hands,
a broad one;
sentences.i: and at once he heaped up a broad bed for himself with his own hands;
sentences.n: ἐπαμήσατο is the aorist of ἐπαμάω 'heap up'; χερσὶ φίλῃσιν, 'with his own dear hands', uses φίλος in its common possessive sense, as regularly with parts of the body in Homer.

sentences.t:
φύλλων γὰρ ἔην χύσις ἤλιθα πολλή,
ὅσσον τ’ ἠὲ δύω ἠὲ τρεῖς ἄνδρας ἔρυσθαι
ὥρῃ χειμερίῃ, εἰ καὶ μάλα περ χαλεπαίνοι.
sentences.tr:
phyllōn gar eēn chysis ēlitha pollē,
hosson t’ ēe dyō ēe treis andras erysthai
hōrēi cheimeriēi, ei kai mala per chalepainoi.
sentences.i: for there was a great heap of fallen leaves, enough to shelter two or even three men in the season of winter, however hard it might be raging.
sentences.n: ἔρυσθαι is an epic infinitive of ἔρυμαι 'guard, shelter'. ὅσσον τε again carries the epic τε of a standing measure, 'as much as would…', already met at line 400 of this part. ὥρῃ χειμερίῃ, 'in the wintry season', with εἰ … χαλεπαίνοι, an optative of a general condition, describes the leaf-pile's normal, all-weather capacity to shelter men, not one particular storm.

sentences.t:
τὴν μὲν ἰδὼν γήθησε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς,
ἐν δ’ ἄρα μέσσῃ λέκτο, χύσιν δ’ ἐπεχεύατο φύλλων.
sentences.tr:
tēn men idōn gēthēse polytlas dios Odysseus,
en d’ ara messēi lekto, chysin d’ epecheuato phyllōn.
sentences.l:
Seeing it, rejoiced much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus,
and in the middle he lay down, and a heap he poured over himself, of leaves.
sentences.i: Much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus was glad to see it, and he lay down in the middle of it and heaped the leaves over himself.
sentences.n: πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς keeps unchanged the whole fixed name-formula, 'much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus'. λέκτο is a rare aorist middle of λέχομαι 'lie down' (a different root from λέγω 'gather, say'). ἐπεχεύατο is the aorist middle of ἐπιχέω 'pour over', here of leaves rather than liquid, echoing χύσις 'a pouring, a heap' just used of the leaf-pile itself.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτε τις δαλὸν σποδιῇ ἐνέκρυψε μελαίνῃ
ἀγροῦ ἐπ’ ἐσχατιῆς, ᾧ μὴ πάρα γείτονες ἄλλοι,
σπέρμα πυρὸς σώζων, ἵνα μή ποθεν ἄλλοθεν αὔοι,
ὣς Ὀδυσεὺς φύλλοισι καλύψατο·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hote tis dalon spodiēi enekrypse melainēi
agrou ep’ eschatiēs, hōi mē para geitones alloi,
sperma pyros sōzōn, hina mē pothen allothen auoi,
hōs Odyseus phylloisi kalypsato·
sentences.l:
And as when someone a brand in black ashes has hidden,
at the edge of a field, for whom there are no other neighbours near,
saving a seed of fire, so that from nowhere else he need kindle it,
so Odysseus in leaves covered himself;
sentences.i: And just as a man on an outlying farm, with no neighbours near, buries a live brand in black ashes to keep a seed of fire alive, so that he need not go and kindle it from some other source, so Odysseus now covered himself with leaves;
sentences.n: A third and final simile closes the part, matching Odysseus's self-burial in leaves to a farmer banking his hearth-fire overnight. δαλός is a 'firebrand', σποδιή 'ashes'; σπέρμα πυρὸς σώζων, 'saving a seed of fire', is a vivid, exact idiom for keeping embers alive under ash so the fire need not be relit from a neighbour's hearth, fixed now for both layers as a likely recurring image, see new-renderings.md. αὔοι is an optative of a rare verb, perhaps 'kindle' (a different word from the common αὔω 'shout'); the exact form is uncertain.

sentences.t:
τῷ δ’ ἄρ’ Ἀθήνη
ὕπνον ἐπ’ ὄμμασι χεῦ’, ἵνα μιν παύσειε τάχιστα
δυσπονέος καμάτοιο φίλα βλέφαρ’ ἀμφικαλύψας.
sentences.tr:
tōi d’ ar’ Athēnē
hypnon ep’ ommasi cheu’, hina min pauseie tachista
dysponeos kamatoio phila blephar’ amphikalypsas.
sentences.l:
and upon him then Athena
sleep over his eyes poured, so that she might make him cease most quickly
from his painful weariness, his dear eyelids having covered all around.
sentences.i: and Athena poured sleep down over his eyes, so as to free him as quickly as possible from his painful weariness, by closing his dear eyelids all around.
sentences.n: χεῦ(ε) is an unaugmented aorist of χέω 'pour'; sleep 'poured over the eyes' is a standing Homeric way of describing the onset of sleep. δυσπονής, 'hard-toiling, painful', is built on δυσ- and πόνος 'toil'. ἀμφικαλύψας, the aorist participle of ἀμφικαλύπτω 'cover round about', closes the part by echoing κάλυψεν, the verb used of the wave that nearly drowned him at line 435 — Odysseus is now covered gently, by sleep and leaves together, rather than dangerously, by the sea.
